Harold Philip Milavsky, 353396 Alberta Inc.; and Gregory Milavsky,
Dwayne Lashyn and Charlene Molotsky, each as Trustees of each of the Harold
Milavsky Family Trust, H. Milavsky Residential Trust, The Harold Milavsky
Grandchildren’s Trust and Harold P. Milavsky Descendants’ Trust

Defendants

_______________________________________________________

Memorandum of
Judgment

of the

Honourable
Mr. Justice

P.J. McIntyre

_______________________________________________________

[
1
]

The Defendants ask for a confidentiality order
about financial documents and information that must be disclosed in these
actions. The Plaintiff asks that the Defendants be compelled to answer
questions that were refused or taken under advisement during a
cross-examination on affidavits of Dwayne Lashyn, the executor of the estate of
Harold Milavsky, filed in support of the Defendants’ application for summary
dismissal of the Plaintiff’s claims against the Residential Trust.

Background

[
2
]

Harold Milavsky and Marilyn Milavsky lived
together from 1990 in a residence known as the Eau Claire condominium. They
were common-law partners for 9 years, and 10 years a married couple.

[
3
]

These two actions arise from their relationship.
In 2009 Marilyn filed a divorce and matrimonial property action against Harold.
In 2010 she filed an unjust enrichment and constructive trust action against
Harold, 4 trusts, and an Alberta numbered company 353396, as trustee of the
Residential trust to which Harold had given the Eau Claire condominium in 1992.
(Collectively the “Trust Defendants”)

[
4
]

Harold became incompetent October 2009. He died
December 4, 2012.

[
5
]

In May 2011 Hawco J. summarily dismissed
Marilyn’s claim against the Trust Defendants, except for the Descendants’ trust
which had not sought summary judgment. In July 2011 the Court of Appeal allowed
Marilyn’s appeal from that Order:
Milavsky v. Milavsky

2011 ABCA 231
.

[
6
]

In February 2012 I dismissed Harold’s
application to remove Laurie Allen as counsel for Marilyn. In May 2012 I was
appointed case manager. In October 2012 I dismissed Harold’s application for
severance of the issues of liability and damages. In July 2013 the Court of
Appeal dismissed Harold’s appeal from that order:
Milavsky v. 353396

2013 ABCA 253
.

[
7
]

The two matters are now set for trial, to be
heard together October 5, 2015 for 8 weeks. The Residential Trust also seeks
summary dismissal of Marilyn’s claim, relying in part on recent affidavits
sworn by Lashyn (he has sworn 13 affidavits). That application will be heard in
January 2015, or earlier if time becomes available.

Confidentiality application

[
8
]

The parties’ positions on confidentiality have
evolved.

[
9
]

The Trust Defendants first applied for an order
sealing the court file. This was modified to ask for an order permitting only
counsel to see documents, not Marilyn. Now the Defendants propose an order that
would require Marilyn to apply to court if she wanted to refer to what the
Defendants characterize as confidential information. Mr. McDonald on behalf of
individual trustees suggests as an alternate that confidential documents be
sealed so the public record would contain only unsealed documents or redacted
affidavits.

[
10
]

Marilyn originally refused to consent to any
order, saying the implied undertaking that parties not use documents or
information obtained for collateral matters is sufficient. She now suggests
that an order extend the implied undertaking, which binds parties and counsel,
to third parties such as legal assistants and third-party service providers.
Further, she undertakes that any affidavit filed by the Plaintiff would be
served on the Defendants within 24 hours so that they might then make any
application they wish in respect of the confidentiality of any information
contained in the affidavit.

Case Law

[
11
]

The Defendants’ application touches on three
tensions:

•

privacy rights of litigants in respect of
discovery,

•

open courts in respect of documents filed, and

•

the sufficiency of the implied undertaking.

[
12
]

Is the implied undertaking adequate? Alberta
cases have held the implied undertaking adequate:
Canada Deposit Insurance
Corp. v. Canadian Commercial Bank
, (1990)
1990 CanLII 5885 (AB QB)
, 106 A.R. 205, per Wachowich J.
(as he then was):

7 The Defendant’s response is that the Order
is inappropriate when the law already recognizes and imposes a duty of
confidentiality for any information gained through the discovery process. The
Applicant’s proposed Order is therefore said to be costly, detailed and an
impediment to the action. Most importantly, it is said to be factually
unjustified according to established case law. After surveying the state of the
law in Alberta, I have come to agree with the Defendant’s position.

...

16 While I accept that certain particulars
concerning C.C.B.’s former and present customers may be confidential in nature,
this fact alone is insufficient reason to require anything more explicit from
the Defendants and their counsel than the undertakings which have already been
implied at law.

[
13
]

He did impose an undertaking on clerical staff
who may not have been caught by the undertaking.

[
14
]

In
Murphy Oil Co. v. Predator Corp
.,
2002
ABQB 992
McMahon J. held:

16 In the result the evidence does not
establish unusual circumstances or real risk of abuse. It is not uncommon for
competitors to litigate and for one or both of them to look to the implied
undertaking to protect them against misuse of information revealed. The
information here is very technical. The input of the client will be essential
to counsel even for the purpose of retaining and instructing experts. The
proposed order would also require that advance notice be given as to which
confidential documents or information were going to be referred to at trial C
thus frustrating counsel’s ability to cross-examine the other party’s witnesses
or experts with maximum effect.

[
15
]

Justice Binnie spoke in
Doucette (Litigation
Guardian of) v. Wee Watch Day Care

2008 SCC 8
of the reason for the implied
undertaking:

25 The public interest in getting at the
truth in a civil action outweighs the examinee’s privacy interest, but the
latter is nevertheless entitled to a measure of protection. The answers and
documents are compelled by statute solely for the purpose of the civil action
and the law thus requires that the invasion of privacy should generally be
limited to the level of disclosure necessary to satisfy that purpose and that
purpose alone.

[
16
]

He described its scope as follows:

27  For good reason, therefore, the law
imposes on the parties to civil litigation an undertaking to the court not to
use the documents or answers for any purpose other than securing justice in the
civil proceedings in which the answers were compelled (whether or not such
documents or answers were in their origin confidential or incriminatory in
nature).

[
17
]

The implied undertaking is an onerous
obligation. Intentional breach could result in dismissal of the suits:

29 Breach of the undertaking may be remedied
by a variety of means including a stay or dismissal of the proceeding, or
striking a defence, or, in the absence of a less drastic remedy, contempt
proceedings for breach of the undertaking owed to the court.

[
18
]

At paragraphs 21 and 22 he distinguished the
implied undertaking from the open court principle, noting that pre-trial
discovery is private, and not conducted in court. The documents are thus not
available to the public:

21 ... The only point at which the “open
court” principle is engaged is when, if at all, the case goes to trial and the
discovered party’s documents or answers from the discovery transcripts are
introduced as part of the case at trial. ...

[
19
]

Binnie J. was not dealing with issues about
filing affidavits that may disclose information obtained during questioning.

[
20
]

That the open court principle applies to
documents filed in court can be seen in
Edmonton Journal (The) v. Alberta
(Attorney General)
, 1989 SCC 133:

86   It is equally important for the press
to be able to report upon and for the citizen to receive information pertaining
to court documents. It was put in this way by Anne Elizabeth Cohen in her
article “Access to Pretrial Documents Under the First Amendment” (1984), 84
Colum. L. Rev. 1813, at p. 1827:

“Access to pretrial documents furthers
the same societal needs served by open trials and pretrial civil and criminal
proceedings. Court officials can be better evaluated when their actions are
seen by informed, rather than merely curious, spectators.”

It is against this background, which
recognizes the crucial importance of both the freedom of expression and the
openness of courts, that s. 30 of the Alberta Judicature Act must be
considered.

[
21
]

Thus, affidavits filed in support of motions,
and underlying documents that are necessary to support the motions, should be
open to public scrutiny.
Edmonton Journal
provides a compelling reason
why motion material filed before trial should be accessible.

Analysis

[
22
]

The parties agree that rule 5.3 implicitly
allows for confidentiality order. The onus is on the Trust Defendants to show
on a balance of probabilities that there is a compelling reason for
confidentiality order, and that the danger in disclosure is grossly
disproportionate to the benefit to the Plaintiff:
HRC Tool and Die Mfg. Ltd.
v. Naderi
2013 ABQB 429
at para
8
.

[
23
]

The Trust Defendants say that disclosure would
be contrary to Harold’s wishes that his children and grandchildren not know
that they will receive funds, believing that such knowledge would curb their
ambition. There are 5 children and 12 grandchildren between the ages of 10 and
27. Five of the grandchildren are minors.

[
24
]

The Trust Defendants also suggest that
disclosure would cause a risk to the safety of the beneficiaries. The concern
about danger to the beneficiaries is said to be supported by the kidnapping of
the daughter of a family friend in 1972 (the Hashman kidnapping) and by a
newspaper report of the 1982 plan by two members of the Ku Klux Klan to bomb
the Jewish Community Centre and Harold’s home. Apparently anti-Semitism was the
motivating factor.

[
25
]

Lashyn confirmed in cross-examination on
affidavit that there are no credible or specific threats to any member of
Harold’s family.

[
26
]

An argument about potential harm to the assets
of the trust was abandoned during the course of questioning by the court.

Conclusion on Confidentiality

[
27
]

There is information in the public domain that
would suggest that the beneficiaries of these trusts will receive significant
funds.

[
28
]

It is known that Harold gave $6.3 million to the
Family trust. In 1992, Harold gave the Eau Claire condominium, in which he and
Marilyn had lived since 1990, to the Residential Trust.

[
29
]

Harold gave the Descendants’ Trust $3.3 million.

[
30
]

There is no evidence that Marilyn has acted
improperly with respect to any information that she has obtained over the
course of the years that these lawsuits have been outstanding.

[
31
]

Although the Court understands Harold’s wish
about confidentiality in respect of the amount of funds that may come to the
beneficiary for their benefit, the type of order sought by the applicants is
grossly disproportionate to the benefit could be achieved by respecting
Harold’s wishes. There is no evidence of profligacy following the release of
the information in the public domain to which I have earlier referred.

[
32
]

The arguments by the applicants about possible
physical harm to the beneficiaries are remote, speculative, and unsupported by
evidence.

[
33
]

There is no evidence of harm to the assets of
the trusts.

[
34
]

The form of order proposed by the applicants is
detrimental to Marilyn’s ability to litigate this complex matter. Further, it
places the onus on Marilyn to demonstrate that documents the Defendants choose
to call confidential are not. This misplaces the burden.

[
35
]

The implied undertaking, supplemented by an
order that extends that undertaking to employees of the law firms and
third-party service providers, and that requires affidavits to be served on the
other party within 24 hours of filing, is sufficient to protect the concerns of
the applicants and to preserve the open court principle.

Application to compel answers

[
36
]

The answers refused relate to the source of
contributions to the Eau Claire condominium. The Plaintiff asked who had paid
for the expenses of the condominium. The answer was Harold. On an undertaking
to provide documentary support for this answer Lashyn provided invoices,
receipts, redacted Visa statements, and cancelled cheques. The question now is
whether Quantico, a company associated with Harold, reimbursed him for those
payments. Lashyn, an accountant responsible for Harold’s affairs says he was not
reimbursed. The Plaintiff wants to test this.

[
37
]

I will not require these questions to be
answered. There is no evidence of any practice of reimbursement to Harold.
Lashyn produced Visa statements, receipts and checks to support payments for
the upkeep of the Eau Claire condominium. Lashyn, in his affidavit, has sworn
that there was no reimbursement. There is no evidence to trigger what is
essentially an audit of visa and bank statements to check this response.
Further this is a remote issue on the application by the Residential Trust for
summary judgment. Should evidence later be found that supports some practice of
reimbursement, and such issue remains important, and not collateral, the
Plaintiff may revisit that question. For now, this line of inquiry raises the
concern about floodgates identified by Slatter J. as he then was in
Weatherill
(Estate) v. Weatherill

2003 ABQB 69
at para
140
. Nor am I satisfied there
is a rational strategy in which these additional documents play a material part
(
Weatherill
, para
16
). Further, it casts too wide a net to say
credibility is always in issue.

[
38
]

I therefore grant an Order as described above on
the confidentiality application. I deny the application to compel further
answers about expenses for the condominium.

Heard on the
22
nd
day of May,
2014 and the 23
rd
day of May, 2014.
